newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil prices flat as refiner demand may fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil prices flat as refiner demand may fall.

text.p: World oil markets were little changed on Tuesday as faltering profit margins at refineries took the shine off a rally that has lifted prices 10 percent this month.
London futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend were up eight cents at $20.24 at 1513 GMT on Tuesday compared with levels below $18 on May 2.
Refinery margins have been squeezed because the price of gasoline has failed to keep pace with the rally in crude oil.
Some dealers expect less sophisticated refiners to trim crude runs in an attempt to stem losses.
The tighter margins "will lead to serious discussions in a number of refineries this week including ours," said a trader at one of Rotterdam's largest plants.
The rally was triggered by fund buying and better fundamentals which included tighter North Sea supplies and growing refinery demand after the end of seasonal spring maintenance.
Markets have also found some support from further delays in new North Sea oilfield projects.
Summer maintenance at North Sea oilfields is expected to trim some 260,000 barrels a day (bpd) from liftings in June at 4.35 million bpd compared to 4.61 million for May.
Analysts said oil markets now were looking finely balanced but that the chances of a supply-led price slump have receded.
Dealers were expecting Tuesday's U.S. oil inventory figures released by the American Petroleum Institute to give a directional kick after unexpectedly large stock builds in last week's data.
Gasoline figures are of particular interest ahead of the U.S. summer driving season. Demand from U.S. motorists is often enough to lift world oil prices.
Dealers are also watching the United Nations' oil-for-food exchange closely. Some expect higher oil prices to translate into a cancellation of some Iraqi crude liftings under the deal.

Under the plan Iraq is permitted to sell $2 billion worth of crude over six months ending June 9. Last week's higher prices mean the financial target may be met more quickly than had been anticipated.
No liftings of Iraqi Kirkuk have been set for the final two weeks of the first 180 day period of the deal which indicates Baghdad is close to its cash target.
